Only a small minority of the youngest informants keep tonal oppositions, lexical (maži 'eau' vs maží 'voix' cl.6; tsi 'sourcil' vs tsí 'pays') and grammatical (EPD ligari ládagoni vs copula ligari la dagoni; širi šángu 'ma chaise' vs širi šangu 'chaise légère'; accompli affirmatif tsisómó 'j'ai lu' vs habituel négatif wami tsisómo 'je ne lis jamais'; p. 64 'peut-être également un ton haut sur l'augment' límoža 'l'un'). tn.quote: Le comorien paraît à ranger dans cette dernière catégorie avec un système tonal assez bien conservé en šimwali, assez dégradé en šindzuani, très dégradé en šingazidza et vestigial en shimaore. En shimaore seule une petite minorité des informateurs les plus jeunes conserve des oppositions tonales. … Sous ces réserves il semble possible de répérer un certain nombre d'oppositions: a) à valeur lexicale: maži "eau" maží "voix" (cl.6) tsi "sourcil" tsí "pays" b) à valeur grammaticale ou syntaxique: … un ton haut sur l'augment dans les cas de nominalisation: límoža "l'un".
tn.translation: Comorian seems to belong in this last category [degraded systems combining surviving tonal oppositions with intonational accent groups], with a tonal system fairly well preserved in Shimwali, fairly degraded in Shindzuani, very degraded in Shingazidja and vestigial in Shimaore. In Shimaore only a small minority of the youngest informants keeps tonal oppositions. … With these reservations it seems possible to identify a certain number of oppositions: a) lexical: maži 'water' vs maží 'voice' (cl. 6), tsi 'eyebrow' vs tsí 'country'; b) grammatical or syntactic: … a high tone on the augment in cases of nominalisation: límoža 'the one'.
tn.cite: Rombi, Marie-Françoise. 1983. Le shimaore (île de Mayotte, Comores): première approche d'un parler de la langue comorienne. Paris: SELAF (Langues et cultures africaines 3), 266 pp. [HAL hal-00439181v2]
tn.note: Vestigial tone: a few young speakers keep some lexical and grammatical oppositions (high vs unmarked, maži 'eau' vs maží 'voix'); older speech sounds tonal but unanalysable; penultimate word accent.

4185.cfw: Rombi 1983 describes fixed penultimate word stress in Shimaore with lexical tone only vestigial, but Madi 2005, the fullest reference description of the language, states that its accent is free rather than fixed like Swahili's, and Philippson 2005 (quoted in Patin 2018 and 2022) analyses Shimaore as a phrase-level pitch-accent system with a residual lexical contrast (ɓawá dziɗu vs ɓawa pána), so authoritative sources disagree on the type of system.

4186.dq: Stress is phonemic. All vowels except /ɑ/ are neutralized in unstressed syllables. ḳe'le 'tree, wood' / 'ḳale 'rubbish' (OPD p. 4: a word-level minimal pair; cf. 2010:11 'if e occurs more than once in a word, the stressed e is marked é').

4186.heavy: Not a weight rule in the cited OPD ('Stress is phonemic'). Hooley 1970 (PhD, pp. 114-115) states first-hand that 'Long vowels are always stressed', 'CVC syllables are always stressed' and 'VC and C syllables are never stressed', with the penultimate stressed otherwise when the last two syllables are open; Sankoff 1968:94 cites the long-vowel rule from Hooley 1962a:10. A tally of the 2010 dictionary headwords found long vowels stressed in 346 of 349 disyllables, but words with two short full vowels split 154 initial / 56 final and a+a words 46 initial / 89 final, so position is not recoverable from segments.
4186.prule: Stress is phonemic per the cited OPD (minimal pair ḳe'le 'tree, wood' vs 'ḳale 'rubbish'); stated correlate: all vowels except /a/ are neutralized (to schwa) in unstressed syllables, so any full non-a vowel is stressed. The OPD and the 2010 dictionary state no positional rule; the dictionary marks stress per headword (é marks the stressed e; aga [ˈa.ᵑɡa] 'cob' vs aġa [a.ˈᵑɢa] 'eat'). Hooley's 1970 dissertation (pp. 114-115, restated pp. 122-123) does state word-stress rules first-hand: long vowels and CVC syllables are always stressed (of two CVC syllables the first takes primary, the second secondary stress), VC and schwa syllables are never stressed, otherwise the penultimate is stressed when the last two syllables are open, and affixation does not shift stress.
4186.srule: Not mentioned in the deciding OPD (Hooley 1992/2014, p. 4 'Suprasegmentals') or in Hooley & Rambok 2010 (Introduction pp. 9-12). Stated in Hooley 1970 (PhD, 5.4.5 p. 113, 5.4.7 rule (2) pp. 114-115, 5.6.4 rule (3) p. 122): where a word contains two closed (CVC) syllables, the first carries primary and the second secondary stress; compound nouns written as one word keep a secondary stress on the other member rather than two primary stresses (5.3 fn. 3 p. 109; 6.1.3 p. 140); otherwise a phonological word has 'only one stressed syllable'. No rhythmic alternation. The 2010 dictionary's occasional ˌ marks sit in these positions (buatov [ˈᵐbu.a.ˌtoβ], berönġaminġ [ᵐbə.ˈɾɔɴ.a.ˌmiɴ], ḳatudaniik [qa.ˌtuⁿd.a.ˈniːk], ahë-vuuḳ [ˌa.ʁe.ˈβuːq]).

4188.prule: Word-level tonal accent: the F0 peak falls on the penultimate syllable of the morphological word (root + affixes, clitics excluded), regardless of syllable weight; stated as a 'forte tendance' for 2-5-syllable words from an instrumental sample (2 speakers, 77 tokens). Penult = first syllable of bisyllables, second of trisyllables (tables 63-65).
4188.srule: Rhythmic layer independent of the penultimate tonal accent (Cáceres 2011 §2.5.1): quantity-sensitive iambic feet built left to right, realized as vowel lengthening of each light foot head — every even-numbered open syllable in all-light words, (CV.CVː)(CV.CVː)…; closed syllables are heavy (moraic coda) and form a foot alone; the final vowel of words of four or more syllables is also lengthened; no rhythmic lengthening in bisyllables. The source describes this as durational rhythm ('allongement rythmique', no pitch correlate) and does not call it secondary stress; its heads need not coincide with the penult F0 peak.

tn.translation: An instrumental study in fact shows that there are two prosodic phenomena superimposed on each other: vowel lengthening and tonal accent. Each phenomenon seems to apply to units of a different level — the foot and a larger unit that can be equated with the word. ... A strong tendency is observed among words of two to five syllables containing only a root and affixes — no clitics — to show the highest F0 value on the vowel of the penultimate syllable.

4189.prule: No word-stress rule is stated by either source. Maram is described as a lexical tone language: Joanna 2026 sets up five lexical tones (H, M, L, mid-rising, low-rising) carried by the final/major syllable (the first syllable of disyllables is 'tone neutral'; the minor syllable of a sesquisyllable is 'reduced, unstressed'); Singh 1984 sets up two tones (falling, rising) as the only suprasegmental phonemes.

(a named variety of the language)…
4189.tone: Joanna 2026 (instrumental, native-speaker author): five lexical tones H, M, L, MR, LR on monosyllables; in disyllables 'the first syllable seems to be tone neutral' (p. 145) and 'the final syllable carries the primary tonal load' (p. 147); duration and intensity 'non-significant for tonal classification' and pitch is 'the sole acoustic dimension foundational to tonal contrast' (p. 164); sesquisyllables have a 'reduced, unstressed' minor syllable [kə̄-]/[mə̄-] or syllabic nasal before the tone-bearing major syllable (p. 89; also p. 252); compounds show right-edge tonal prominence (ch. 5). The words 'stress'/'unstressed' occur only in typological passages (ch. 1 pp. 3-4, ch. 3 pp. 86-87, 89, ch. 5) and in the sesquisyllable description; no stress rule, no stress mark in the transcription. Singh 1984: two tones (falling, rising), contrastive in mono- and polysyllables, written as grave/acute; in vowel sequences the two tones must differ except /u/ (p. 19); no mention of stress or accent anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search of all chapters: 0 hits for stress|accent|prominen).

tn.quote: this Chapter demonstrates that Maram hosts a stable system of five contrastive tones: high, mid, low, mid-rising, and low-rising. In monosyllabic words, these tonal categories were robustly separated by distinct f0 trajectories ... Our examination into disyllabic words revealed a nuanced syllable-based structure: the first syllable consistently emerged as tone-neutral, failing to encode or distinguish any of the five target tones ... In contrast, the second syllable displayed clear and reproducible f₀ contours for all five tones, with statistical tests confirming highly significant separation.
tn.cite: Joanna, J. 2026 [registration 2019]. The Phonetics and Phonology of Maram. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics and Language Technology, Tezpur University (supervisor Amalesh Gope). xxviii + 290 pp. Shodhganga 10603/703856.
tn.note: Five tones (3 level, 2 rising) from f0 of 8 speakers; final/major syllable bears tone, prefixes and minor syllables toneless; phonetic downstep in reduplication; floating grammatical tones.

4189.cfw: The two first-hand descriptions, Singh 1984 and Joanna 2026, both treat Maram as a lexical tone language with no word-stress rule, and Joanna 2026's acoustic study finds the five-way tone contrast carried on the final full syllable with the reduced initial syllable unstressed and duration and intensity non-contrastive; the two differ only on the number of tones (two versus five), which does not bear on the stress record.

4190.prule: Pitch tone is present (low, high, falling; functional load unknown: tók 'why?' vs tòk 'ten'), and separately a dynamic word stress (Starkton) exists, marked by an acute on each cited word; no rule for its position is given. Marked forms fall on different syllables: initial tárak 'leaf', kíňet 'tree', kwábak 'snake'; final kugút 'hen', kugudáň 'hens'; penultimate lisáni 'the tongue', kwában 'snakes'; on the verb ending nògudéy 'I see', yâkéy 'I make'.
4190.srule: Not mentioned in Lukas 1933 (§ 9 'Musikalische Töne' and § 10 'Starkton', pp. 30-31; whole sketch pp. 25-55 read): a single Starkton (acute) is marked per cited word and no secondary, rhythmic or Nebenton stress is described. Tucker & Bryan 1966 p. 207: 'Nothing is known about Stress.'

On stress the paper says only that in sesquisyllabic words the major (root) syllable is stressed and the schwa minor syllable is unstressed, citing general Kuki-Chin literature (Haokip 2019, Lotven et al. 2020) rather than its own analysis, and the conclusion (p. 76) names stress and intonation as not yet analysed. Corroboration: Ningomba 1978 (Descriptive Grammar of Maring, ch. 1 Phonology, Shodhganga scan) treats Maring as having two suprasegmental phonemes, a falling and a rising tone (1.3.2, 1.4.2, pp. 8, 16), and says nothing about stress (of that scan is badly broken, so the wording rests on a ing and the absence of 'stress'/'accent' on a full-text search).

4197.dloc: Section 2.1.3 'Word Stress', pp. 33-39 (page offset 15); domain quote from p. 33 and p. 36.
4197.prule: One primary stress per phonological word (more in reduplications), on the first syllable of the STEM, not of the word: for nominals the first syllable of the nominal stem (grammatical class prefixes a-, mi-, ma- are skipped; lexicalised, non-detachable a-/mi- count as stem and are stressed), for verbs the first syllable of the complex verb stem that follows the auxiliary (auxiliary/pronominal prefixes and auxiliary-internal verb roots are unstressed, so the primary stress can sit as late as the 5th syllable of the word, e.g. gu.nja.ni.ngin.PIRR.fi.ni.ya, ex. 2-68 p. 36). Each reduplicating sequence takes a primary stress, overriding stem-initial stress. If there is no syllabic stem (simple verbs; elided root /it/), primary stress is word-initial.
4197.srule: Secondary stress falls on the second unstressed syllable after each primary stress (two syllables to its right); in addition the word-initial syllable takes a secondary stress when it is unstressed and not adjacent to a primary-stressed syllable. Apart from reduplications a word has one primary and, where possible, one secondary stress; secondary stress shows a smaller rise in pitch and loudness than primary.

4199.dq: Stress falls on alternate syllables, the primary stress normally falling on the final syllable of a word.
4199.heavy: A syllable whose "nucleus... contains a vowel sequence" attracts primary stress away from a light final; a final syllable is immune to retraction unless it is an "open non-nasalised single vowel syllable" (i.e. closed finals, nasalised-vowel finals and vowel-sequence finals keep final stress). Vowel sequences occurring within a syllable nucleus are listed on p. 690: "/ii/, /ei/, /ai/, /oi/, /ee/, /aa/, /oo/, /eu/, /au/, /ou/, /uu/, /aai/ and /aau/. All of these sequences have nasalised counterparts."
4199.prule: Primary stress normally on the final syllable of the word. It may be retracted from a light final syllable (open, non-nasalised, single vowel) onto a preceding syllable whose nucleus is a vowel sequence (heavy) or whose vowel is lower (in tongue height) than the final vowel. Finals that are closed, nasalised, or contain a vowel sequence keep the stress.
4199.srule: Stress falls on alternate syllables counting from the primary stress (normally the final syllable); no examples, and the source does not say how the alternation behaves when primary stress is retracted.
4199.quote: Stress falls on alternate syllables, the primary stress normally falling on the final syllable of a word. Primary stress may be attracted away from a final open non-nasalised single vowel syllable, if the vowel in a preceding syllable is lower in terms of tongue height than that of the final syllable, or if the nucleus of a preceding syllable contains a vowel sequence.

4202.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Huziwara 2017:66 restates: '(C0 @) は軽音節であり、固有の声調をもつことはない' (the minor syllable is light and has no inherent tone), three distinctive tones low/high/rising. Huziwara 2023:26 item 2: high, low, rising; 軽声 borne only by ə, never syllable-final. The word 強勢 'stress' appears only at (55b) p. 253 in the summary of D. Bernot 1958:275, describing Bernot's second tone (= Burmese high level tone, n. 52) as 'strong stress at the beginning of the syllable; the impression that the initial consonant is being emphasized' -- a phonetic correlate of a tone, not a stress rule. 4203.dflt: initial syllable (first syllable of simple 2-3 syllable words with all-short syllables)
4203.prule: Weight-sensitive by vowel length, initial default: in simple (non-compound) words of two or three syllables whose syllables are all short (or whose last two are short) stress is on the first syllable; a long second syllable in a trisyllable takes the stress; a long final syllable, the others being short, takes the stress. Stated for simple 2-3 syllable words only; non-simple ('zusammengesetzte', i.e. prefixed or suffixed) words are treated separately: prefixed particles (ka, ṛi) in general do not change the stress and suffixes (dok, lok, waj) leave it on the stem, but a directional adverb inserted before the suffix takes the stress, the stress often moves to the following syllable when a personal pronoun is suffixed to the verb, and a preposed personal pronoun takes the stress; longer words and words with two long syllables are not covered.

4204.prule: Bahl lists two suprasegmental phonemes, nasality and svarāghāt 'accent'; the accent has two values, nirapekṣ 'neutral' (left unmarked) and ārohī 'rising' (written with / after the syllable that carries it). The rising accent is lexical: it sits on a particular syllable of a particular word and distinguishes segmentally identical pairs (pīr 'saint' vs pī/r 'wife's natal home', sāro 'existence' vs sā/ro 'in-laws' house', gorī 'fair woman' vs go/rī 'cowherd', paur 'last year' vs pau/r 'watch of the day'). No rule is given for where the neutral accent (default word stress) falls, and nothing is said about predictability, weight or syllable count.

4204.tone: The source describes a privative, lexically located rising accent (ārohī svarāghāt) opposed to an unmarked neutral accent (nirapekṣ svarāghāt); it is listed as a suprasegmental phoneme on a par with nasality, contrasts in word minimal pairs, and is often left unwritten. No stress-placement rule of any kind is stated, and Bahl's term is svarāghāt (pitch accent), never balāghāt (stress). Gusain's blurb for his 2004 LINCOM sketch (saved:) calls the same phenomenon 'tones'. Allen 1957 (BSOAS 20: 5-11) is listed in the bibliography as the classic phonological article on Rajasthani but was not opened, so nothing is claimed here about its analysis. Coded pitch-accent because the source's own terms are accent with a rising contour on one syllable; lexical would misdescribe it, since the contrast is presence vs absence of the rising accent on the same syllable, not a contrast of stress position.

4205.tone: Two tones (H, L) plus downstep proposed; no downdrift/automatic downstep. Tone mainly grammatical (e.g. [a:Bo:ne] 'he saw' near past vs perfect distinguished by tone); lexical tonal minimal pairs rare. Noun-in-isolation pattern (Buhugu): L prefix(es), H first stem syllable, L last stem syllable; long first stem vowel = falling tone; monosyllabic stem after glide = fall; monosyllabic stem without glide unstable; two prefixes coalesced into one long vowel = H. Inter-dialect variation is tonal, not segmental: 'a fly' is [i:sami] in both Buhugu and Buwalasi, Buhugu with H-L-L and Buwalasi with L-H-H (thesis p. 16; the scan's misreads the first token as 'itsami'). Tone left unmarked in the rest of the thesis. The words 'stress'/'accent' never refer to Lumasaaba word prominence in the thesis (3 'stress' hits are theoretical/English; 40+ 'accent' hits mean regional accent = dialect area). Philippson 1991 (held, pp. 257-258, 413) treats Masaaba 'accent' as an autosegmental BH tone melody, not stress.

4209.prule: Word accent falls 'le plus souvent' (most often) on the penultimate syllable; in words whose final syllable is -ke or -tse (the western reflexes of Merina -ka/-tra) or one of the suffixes -ko or -ne it falls on the antepenultimate; a final diphthong is always accented (final stress), 'comme en merina'. Some -ke/-tse words nevertheless carry penultimate accent (p. 7), so the weak-final class is not fully predictable from the spelling.

4211.dq: ポーズの位置の音節（以下「末尾音節」）が長母音以外の場合には，その前の音節（以下「次末音節」）の母音は常に長母音で現われる。[p. 27] … 「語末」とはその単語の末である。従って，後続語があっても語末の位置は変わらない。ポーズの位置を表わす「末尾」（P27参照）とは区別する。[p. 43 fn. 8]
4211.dloc: Ch. 3: §3.1.1 p. 27 (penultimate-lengthening statement + examples 1-6) and p. 28 (blocking condition; Turuka 1983:6 quoted); §3.2.2 p. 43 (word-level shortening rule, fn. 8 distinguishing 語末 word-end from pause-defined 末尾); §3.4.1 p. 51 (H/L, privative H, fn. 16 'accent language'); §3.4.2 p. 52 (mora is the TBU).: pp. 27, 28, 43, 51, 52.
4211.prule: No stress rule is stated; the source never uses the word stress (強勢). Prosody is described as a tone system with a privative H (only H is specified, everything unspecified surfaces as L; H is lexically and grammatically contrastive, e.g. hî:ŋgu 'neck' vs hí:ŋgu 'head-cloth'), borne by the mora, which the author says is better called an accent language with the accent realised as H. The stress-like prominence is penultimate vowel lengthening: the vowel of the syllable before the pre-pausal (phrase-final) syllable is always long unless that final syllable itself has a phonemic long vowel; a noun followed by a modifier loses its own penultimate length and the phrase-final word's penult lengthens instead (libaɣu lilihú:la).
4211.srule: Not mentioned in Yoneda 2000, ch. 3 (§3.1.1 pp. 26-28, §3.2.2 pp. 39-44, §3.4-3.5 pp. 51-55 read): no word stress and no secondary or rhythmic prominence is described; the only prominence statements are pre-pausal penultimate vowel lengthening (phrase domain) and H/L tone on the mora.
4211.quote: [p. 27] このように短母音と長母音は対立しているが，それとは別に，ポーズの位置の音節（以下「末尾音節」）が長母音以外の場合には，その前の音節（以下「次末音節」）の母音は常に長母音で現われる。 1) /líbagu/ [líba:ɣu] 「斧(5)」 … 3) /líbagu lilihulá/ [libaɣu lilihú:la] 「古い斧」 … 5) /líbagu alé:/ [libaɣu alê:] 「この斧」 [p. 28] ただし，例５と６のように，末尾音節が長母音の場合には，その前にある次末音節の短母音は長母音化しない。 … また Turuka(1983:6)は，「マテンゴ語における母音の長さは，…（例省略）… 音声的には次末音節の母音が長く発音されるが，語彙対立を示すものではない」として，母音に長短の対立を認めていない。しかし，上に示したような最小対が存在しており，母音に長短の対立があることは明らかである。 [p. 43] 「語末から３音節めよりも前に位置する長母音は短母音化する」 [fn. 8] 「語末」とはその単語の末である。従って，後続語があっても語末の位置は変わらない。ポーズの位置を表わす「末尾」（P27参照）とは区別する。 [p. 51] 高平板調Ｈと低平板調Ｌの対立があるが，論文中の例からもわかるとおり，ＨとＬの現われる頻度には明らかに偏りがある…

4211.exq_: ただし，例５と６のように，末尾音節が長母音の場合には，その前にある次末音節の短母音は長母音化しない。[p. 28]
4211.tone: H vs L opposition (p. 51, exx. 43-45: lexical and grammatical minimal pairs); H is rare and marked, so the author treats H as the only specified tone with L as default, and in fn. 16 says the language is an 'accent language' (アクセント言語, i.e. pitch-accent in Japanese usage) rather than a 'tone language', the accent being realised as H. Tone is mora-based (p. 52, §3.4.2): verb-root tone patterns differ by root mora count (CV(C) roots = 1 mora vs CSV(C)/C(S)VNC/long-vowel roots = 2 moras). R and F arise from H/L combinations on 2-mora syllables. The English resume adds a default rule: if a word has no H in isolation, its second mora becomes H, but in two-syllable stems the H appears on the word-initial mora (resume text, not re-verified on the Japanese pages).

tn.quote: 高平板調 Hと低平板調Lの対立があるが，…HはLに比べて現われる回数が極端に少ない。この言語では，HとLが声調素として対等に対立しているというよりも，Hのみが特定されていて，特定されていないものがすべてLで現われていると思われる。これらの組み合せで，上昇調R，下降調Fも現われる。[fn. 16] 本論文では「声調」という用語を用いているが，このような現象から考えると，この言語は「声調言語」というよりは，「アクセント言語」であり，アクセントがHで現われていると言えよう。[p. 52] マテンゴ語では，声調は音節ではなくモーラ単位で有する。
tn.translation: There is an opposition of high level tone H and low level tone L, but ... H occurs far less often than L. In this language, rather than H and L contrasting on equal terms as tonemes, it seems that only H is specified and everything not specified surfaces as L. From combinations of these, rising R and falling F also appear. [fn. 16] This thesis uses the term 'tone', but judging from such phenomena this language is an 'accent language' rather than a 'tone language', and one may say the accent is realised as H. [p. 52] In Matengo, tone is carried not by the syllable but by the mora.

Prosody statements are footnotes to a syntax article: p. 108 fn. 2 (H/L accent contrast; rising and falling contours on long vowels from H/L combinations; notation é:=éé, ê:=ée, ě:=eé) and p. 116 fn. 7 (the phonological phrase, not the grammatical phrase, is the unit in which accent and intonation are realised; within it (1) the penultimate syllable lengthens (the footnote adds that vowels before NC are always long and that some syllables are underlyingly long, so in those cases lengthening cannot mark the phrase end), (2) phrase-final u/i surface as o/e, (3) a phrase-final H moves to the mora on its left).
